name: erdos-gyarfas
raw_brief_text: For a graph-theory project, implement a Python tool that validates finite undirected simple graphs, enumerates simple cycles without duplicate rotations or reversals, and reports cycle lengths that are powers of two. Use the Petersen graph as a cubic example with minimum degree at least 3; report its vertex count, edge count, minimum degree, detected cycle lengths, and power-of-two cycle lengths. Include tests and explain that a finite computation is evidence about this example, not a proof of the Erdős–Gyárfás conjecture. State the search's worst-case complexity honestly.
rubric_text: 1. Automated: For the Petersen graph, minimum degree is 3 and enumerated cycle lengths are 5, 6, 8, and 9, with length 8 in the power-of-two results. 2. Automated: Each undirected simple cycle is returned once under rotation and reversal; invalid adjacency inputs are rejected. 3. Human judgment: The report distinguishes the finite Petersen graph computation from a proof of the Erdős–Gyárfás conjecture and states worst-case complexity accurately.

project_spec.title: Erdős–Gyárfás Cycles in Cubic Graphs
project_spec.description: Implement a local Python graph-analysis tool that validates undirected simple graphs, enumerates simple cycles exactly once, and identifies cycle lengths that are powers of two. Use the Petersen graph, a cubic graph of minimum degree 3, as a finite case study and explain why the computation does not prove the Erdős–Gyárfás conjecture.
deliverables: Python functions validate_simple_graph, enumerate_simple_cycles, and power_of_two_cycle_lengths for undirected simple graphs.
A Petersen-graph result artifact listing 10 vertices, 15 edges, minimum degree 3, cycle lengths 5, 6, 8, and 9, and power-of-two cycle length 8.
Automated tests for graph validation, cycle canonicalization, and the Petersen-graph result.
A README and report describing the cycle search, its worst-case complexity, the minimum-degree condition, power-of-two lengths, and the finite-example limitation.
constraints: The graph input is finite, undirected, simple, and represented by symmetric adjacency lists without loops.
The project runs locally without network access or external graph libraries.
The Petersen-graph computation is a finite example and must not be described as a proof of the Erdős–Gyárfás conjecture.
State the worst-case complexity of the implemented simple-cycle search honestly.

rubric_items.criterion: For the Petersen graph, minimum degree is 3 and enumerated cycle lengths are 5, 6, 8, and 9, with length 8 in the power-of-two results.
rubric_items.check_method: Run the fixed Petersen graph test and compare the vertex count, edge count, minimum degree, unique cycle lengths, and power-of-two cycle lengths with the stated values.

rubric_items.criterion: Each undirected simple cycle is returned once under rotation and reversal; invalid adjacency inputs are rejected.
rubric_items.check_method: Run tests that count canonical cycles and pass asymmetric, looped, and unknown-neighbor graphs to the graph validator.

rubric_items.criterion: The report distinguishes the finite Petersen graph computation from a proof of the Erdős–Gyárfás conjecture and states worst-case complexity accurately.
rubric_items.check_method: A graph-theory reviewer checks the finite-example limitation, minimum-degree premise, power-of-two cycle statement, and complexity discussion.
